line/open: A classifier keeps a set of numbers, and each must be chosen well for it to work. How many are there, and what makes that count grow?
line/line: Take the line between cats and ships, drawn from two features. Its two weights, in w, turn it, and its bias, b, slides it.
line/three: Those three numbers are the whole classifier. Choose them, and you have chosen one line out of all the lines you could draw.
line/name: Numbers that pick out one member of a whole family like this are called parameters. You know two already: m and b are the parameters of y equals m x plus b.
line/input: The points are not parameters. They are inputs, a new one with every image: the inputs pass through, and the parameters stay put.
block/D: Now give it more features: D of them, four here. A class weighs every feature, so its weights fill a row of D numbers.
block/C: Each class gets its own row, as in the matrix W. With C classes, three here, W is C rows by D columns.
block/weights: Three rows of four: twelve weights.
block/bias: Then each class adds one bias, in a column beside W: three more.
block/total: Twelve plus three: fifteen parameters. In general, C times D, plus C.
block/shape: As shapes, W is C by D, three by four, and b holds C numbers. Not four by three: each row is dotted with the input, so it needs one weight per feature.
grows/px: Where do the features come from? Often straight from an image, one per pixel. A tiny gray image, two pixels by two, gives four, so D is four.
grows/side: Make it twice as wide and twice as tall, and it has four times the pixels. Every row of W grows four times as long: three times sixteen, plus three, is fifty one.
grows/color: Make it color, and each pixel brings three numbers, for red, green and blue. D triples to forty eight, and so do the weights.
grows/photo: A real photo works the same way, only bigger. A thirty two by thirty two color photo is three thousand and seventy two numbers, so ten classes take ten rows that long, plus ten biases: thirty thousand, seven hundred and thirty parameters.
grows/class: Make it twenty classes instead of ten, and the rows and the biases both double. So does the whole count.
grows/data: What never enters the count is how many images it scores. Ten or a million, W and b keep their shape.
chain/map: Look again at W x plus b: it turns D numbers into C. A rule that carries each input to an output is called a map, and this one, weights times inputs plus a bias, is a linear map.
chain/chain: Its outputs need not be class scores. As with matrices in a chain, one map can hand its outputs to the next: a first map turns the four inputs into numbers in the middle, and a second turns those into the three scores.
chain/H: How many numbers sit in the middle is up to whoever builds it. Call that H: here, five.
chain/W1: The first map has its own weights, W one: one row per output and one column per input, so H by D, five by four.
chain/b1: And its own biases, b one: one per output, so five.
chain/c1: So the first map holds four times five weights, plus five biases: twenty five parameters.
chain/W2: The second map counts the same way. Its weights, W two, are C by H: three by five.
chain/c2: Its biases, b two, are one per class. Fifteen weights plus three biases: eighteen.
chain/sum: Add the two maps: forty three. Each one counts as inputs times outputs, plus one bias per output.
